M9_S01.summary: Rūpa is named from 'breaking up': matter is whatever is deformed and destroyed by conditions, lasting only seventeen mind-moments.
body: Rūpa derives from the root 'rup', to be broken up, to be scattered. Materiality is that which changes its shape and state under the influence of opposing physical conditions such as heat, cold, hardness and softness.
Matter is what is constantly altering and disintegrating. A material phenomenon endures only for seventeen thought-moments, that is, seventeen mind-moments.
The source gives an image: matter changes so quickly that one cannot strike twice in exactly the same place.
The nearest senses of rūpa are therefore: shape, the material part, the physical body, that which has no awareness.

M9_S02.summary: Matter has eight characteristics: rootless, conditioned, object of the taints, constructed, mundane, of the sense sphere, without an object, and not to be eradicated.
body: 1. Rootless (Ahetuka): matter has no connection with roots in the sense of association — no root arises together with it.
2. With conditions (Sappaccaya): matter is bound to four conditions, namely kamma, consciousness, temperature and nutriment.
3. Object of the taints (Sāsava): matter serves as the object on which the taints fasten.
4. Constructed (Saṅkhata): it is put together by the four conditions just named.

5. Mundane (Lokiya): it belongs wholly to the world, the sense sphere and the form sphere. 6. Of the sense sphere (Kāmāvacara): it is the object of sensual craving, the field of the five sense objects. 7. Without an object (Anārammaṇa): matter cannot know an object. 8. Not to be eradicated (Appahātabba): matter is not something the path destroys.

M9_S03.summary: Materiality has two parts: the four great elements and the twenty-four kinds of derived matter, twenty-eight in all.
body: Materiality has two parts: the four great essentials (Mahābhūtāni) and the modifications dependent on them, that is, derived materiality (Upādāyarūpāni).
The great essentials are four: earth (Paṭhavī), water (Āpo), fire (Tejo) and air (Vāyo).
The derived materialities are twenty-four, each of them dependent on the four great essentials and incapable of arising without them.
The total: 24 derived materialities + 4 great essentials = 28 material phenomena.

M9_S04.summary: Earth supports, water coheres, fire is temperature and air is motion; the tangible object consists of three of them, water excepted.
body: Paṭhavī-dhātu, the earth element, from the root 'puth', to extend, to spread out: its characteristic is hardness or softness, and its capacity is to support and bear up the material phenomena arisen with it. Whatever becomes the place on which the co-arisen materialities rest is called earth.
Āpo-dhātu, the water element: the element whose characteristic is to make the material phenomena cohere and hold together.
Tejo-dhātu, the fire element: the element of temperature, which includes both heat and cold.
Vāyo-dhātu, the air element: the element of motion, distension and movement.
Note that the tangible object (phoṭṭhabba) consists of three of the great elements only — earth, fire and air — the water element being excepted, since cohesion cannot be felt by touch.

M9_S05.summary: The twenty-eight material phenomena are set out in eleven groups, from the four great elements to the four characteristics of matter.
body: 1. The great elements (Bhūtarūpa): 4. 2. The sensitive materialities (Pasādarūpa): eye, ear, nose, tongue and body — 5.
3. The objective fields (Gocararūpa): visible form, sound, odour, taste and tangibility. 4. The materiality of sex (Bhāvarūpa): masculinity and femininity — 2.
5. The heart materiality (Hadayarūpa): the heart-base — 1. 6. The life faculty (Jīvitarūpa): the vitality of matter — 1. 7. Nutritive materiality (Āhārarūpa): nutritive essence — 1.
8. The limiting materiality (Paricchedarūpa): the space element, Ākāsa-dhātu — 1. 9. The materialities of intimation (Viññattirūpa): bodily intimation and verbal intimation — 2.

10. The materialities of mutability (Vikārarūpa): lightness (lahutā), malleability (mudutā) and wieldiness (kammaññatā) — 3. 11. The characteristics of matter (Lakkhaṇarūpa): production, continuity, decay and impermanence — 4.
As the source puts it: 'The eleven classes of material phenomena are reckoned as twenty-eight, according to their individual intrinsic characteristics.'

M9_S06.summary: Eighteen material phenomena are concretely produced and ten are not; only the concrete eighteen can serve as objects of insight contemplation.
body: The concretely produced materialities are eighteen: counting from the earth element down to nutritive essence.
The non-concretely produced materialities are ten: from the space element down to impermanence, the last of the four characteristics.

The eighteen concrete materialities are grouped in several ways: as having intrinsic nature (sabhāvarūpa), as possessing the three characteristics (salakkhaṇarūpa), as produced by conditions (nipphannarūpa), as constantly changing (rūparūpa), and as fit to be contemplated by insight (sammasanarūpa).

M9_S07.summary: Matter springs from four origins — kamma produces 18, consciousness 15, temperature 13 and nutriment 12 — and each material phenomenon has its own assigned source.
body: 'Kammaṃ, cittaṃ, utu, āhāro cāti cattāri rūpasamuṭṭhānāni nāma' — material phenomena arise in four ways: from kamma, from consciousness, from temperature and from nutriment.

Matter born of kamma: 18 kinds. Twenty-five wholesome and unwholesome kammas of the sense sphere and form sphere produce kamma-born matter at every mind-moment, beginning with the arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness.

Matter born of consciousness: 15 kinds. Seventy-five cittas — all but the formless resultants and the ten sense consciousnesses — produce mind-born matter, starting from the first life-continuum (bhavaṅga) moment after rebirth.
Matter born of temperature: 13 kinds. The fire element, which includes both heat and cold, produces matter internally and externally once it reaches the moment of presence.
Matter born of nutriment: 12 kinds. Nutritive essence (ojā) produces nutriment-born matter when, in the course of digestion, it reaches the moment of presence.

The assignment of individual phenomena: the heart-base and the faculties are produced by kamma alone; the two intimations by consciousness alone; sound by consciousness and temperature; the three mutabilities — lightness, malleability and wieldiness — by temperature, consciousness and nutriment; the eight inseparables and the space element by all four causes. The four characteristics of matter are produced by no cause at all.
